classIntro.speaker: Kadam Kyle
classIntro.text:
Well done. Aging, sickness and death comes for all of us. Just one little thing.

In the meditation, because it's been a few weeks, what I'm going to do is actually just read the next couple pages that were on in the section because basically the next six pages are just going — bodhichitta! — like that, over and over again. So I'm going to read a few of those pages and then we're just going to develop some admiring faith and wishing faith in bodhisattvas. Thinking, I really admire bodhisattvas and I want to be like them.

Alright, so I just wanted to make that clear. So we'll be starting the class after I read, or at the point that we end in the meditation, after a few of these pages. But when we get to that point, you just sit there and you can listen along, or you can really just try to focus on those two types of faith — really admiring bodhisattvas, really wishing to be one if you're not already. Okay, I think that's it. So we can begin with the prayers.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, Precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace, You, who love all beings without exception, are the source of happiness and goodness. And you guide us to a liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded hands I turn to you, supreme unchanging friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you. May all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy. May everyone be free from misery. May no one ever be separated from their happiness. May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such pure lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind teacher, source of all good; O bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just like the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara's pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma's root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara's ocean; O so that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva's ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the common paths, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy teachers, O bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
Meditation on faith in Bodhisattvas. We can reflect on the following passage. Feel free to follow along, or if you move into a mind of admiring or wishing faith towards Bodhisattvas, then you can just stay with that positive mind and just ignore the rest.

In this world we generally respect and praise a person who repays the kindness he or she has received from another. If this is so, how can we even begin to speak of the great kindness shown by the Bodhisattva — that infinitely compassionate being who benefits others whether or not they have benefited him? Bound by great compassion the Bodhisattva unconditionally helps all sentient beings by leading them in countless ways from suffering to happiness.

Is there any need to speak of the praise and veneration due to such a glorious being? Perhaps there is a person who gives a little food to a few beggars, enough to satisfy them for half a day. Even if they perform this charity with resentment and bad feelings, what is the general reaction to their deeds? The beggars are grateful and the person is praised by others who say they are a great benefactor and have accumulated much virtue. If this is so, then what need is there to speak of the praise and veneration due to the Bodhisattva? This peerless benefactor strives for as long as samsara exists to fulfill not only the temporary wishes of countless sentient beings but also the ultimate aim of bestowing upon them the matchless delights of the awakened ones.

When we understand these reasons well, we should always generate the deepest respect for these Bodhisattvas. By merely rejoicing in their beneficial actions we accumulate boundless merit.

Some may wonder what the Bodhisattva does to practice temporary and ultimate generosity towards others. There are a great variety of possible activities because the Bodhisattva always acts according to the different dispositions of individual beings. Sometimes he or she will benefit others by teaching, sometimes by bestowing material aid, and sometimes by protecting those in danger or great fear. Very advanced Bodhisattvas are able to manifest in different forms according to the needs of others. Depending upon the situation and the need, it is possible for them to manifest as friends, helpers, or even inanimate objects. However, the main way a Bodhisattva benefits others is by teaching them Dharma, for this is the actual method that can lead sentient beings from the sufferings of samsara to the state of highest enlightenment.

But if certain beings lack interest in Dharma, the Bodhisattva will be unable to teach them. Therefore, for these beings they manifest according to their temporary needs. This account of a Bodhisattva's deeds may sound unbelievable, and it may be difficult for us to accept all of this at the present time. But if we become acquainted with and eventually understand the vast Mahayana Dharma, we will realize that a Bodhisattva's deeds are actually like this. Thus first we should listen to Dharma teachings, and afterwards we will begin to understand and appreciate their qualities.

In Tibet, there was a Lama named Pochag Jampa Rinpoche, who had a disciple called Yeshe Gyaltsen. This disciple lived beneath the cave of his teacher and was often without sufficient food and clothing. One day, a nobleman came to visit and offered Yeshe Gyaltsen a sack of barley flour, or tsampa, and some butter. Afterwards, the disciple thought, I must be quite a special person for an aristocrat to give me these offerings.

The next day, Jampa Rinpoche gave teachings. In the middle of his discourse, he said, One of my students is unaware of the fact that a Lama can manifest as tsampa and butter. Then, looking directly at Yeshe Gyaltsen, he continued, This student thinks that it is solely due to his own merits that these provisions are offered to him. Suddenly, Yeshe Gyaltsen realized that both the nobleman and his gifts were all manifestations of his Guru, and a feeling of strong devotion and faith arose in his mind.

Stories such as this one are not easily received by new ears; therefore it may be difficult to accept and believe such things. If we want to know whether a particular food is delicious or not, we can only find out by tasting it. In the same way, it is only by practicing the teachings of Buddha that we will understand the qualities of Dharma. At the moment we have not yet experienced the taste of the Mahayana Dharma, so of course it is difficult to accept. But if we eat this food, we will come to know its taste.

As for the Bodhisattva, his or her ultimate work is to lead all sentient beings to the attainment of enlightenment. To do this, preparation is needed. If we were to invite a king or some other high dignitary to our house, we would make elaborate preparation in advance. In the same way, the Bodhisattva wishes to invite all his guests, the countless mother sentient beings, to the banquet of supreme Buddhahood. He prepares for this now by seeking Buddhahood himself. When he attains this lofty state, he will be able to relieve all sentient beings of their suffering and place them in the bliss of enlightenment. Thus the Bodhisattva is our kindest benefactor, the one who fulfills all our temporary and ultimate wishes.

You can contemplate any of these points and develop a mind of admiring faith or rejoicing in Bodhisattvas, and then gradually turn that into a wishing faith, thinking, I want to become a Bodhisattva. Let that wish be strong in your mind. Hold it single-pointedly. Then, with this wishing faith, we can gradually arise to more practice.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Welcome back, everyone. It's been millennia. We are going to read the excerpt from Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life, page 10 and 11, starting verse 26, chapter 1, through verse 36. Does anyone want to be the lucky reader today? Or the unlucky reader? Mimi, yes, thanks.

shantidevaReading.speaker: Mimi
shantidevaReading.text:
(26) How can we possibly measure the benefits of this jewel of a mind,
The source of joy for all living beings,
And the cure for all their sufferings?

(27) If the mere intention to benefit others
Is more meritorious than making offerings to the Buddhas,
What can be said of actually striving
For the happiness of every single living being?

(28) Although living beings wish to be free from suffering,
They run straight towards the causes of suffering.
And although they wish for happiness,
Out of ignorance they destroy it like a foe.

(29) For those who are deprived of happiness
And afflicted with many sorrows,
Bodhichitta bestows upon them boundless joy,
Eradicates all their suffering, and even dispels their confusion.
Where is there virtue equal to this?
Where is there even such a friend?
Where is there merit such as this?

(30) If even someone who repays a kindness is worthy of some praise,
What can be said of the Bodhisattva who helps others,
Regardless of whether or not they helped him?

(31) If someone regularly, or even just once,
Gives food in a disdainful manner,
Which satisfies a few beings for only half a day,
People honour him or her as virtuous;

(32) So what can be said of one who eternally gives
To countless living beings
The everlasting, unsurpassed bliss of the Sugatas,
Fulfilling all their wishes?

(33) Buddha said that whoever generates an evil mind
Towards a Bodhisattva, a supreme benefactor,
Will remain in hell for as many aeons
As the moments for which that evil mind was generated;

(34) But, for whoever generates a pure mind of faith,
The effects of good fortune will increase even more than that.

(35) Even when Bodhisattvas are faced with great adversity,
Negativity does not arise; rather, their virtues naturally increase.

(36) I prostrate to those who have generated
The holy, precious mind of bodhichitta;
And I go for refuge to those sources of happiness
Who bestow bliss even upon those who harm them.

announcements.speaker: Kadam Kyle
announcements.text:
Thank you very much. A couple of little things, and then we'll get moseying.

One, just a reminder — Kadam Holly is coming to visit us on the 28th, two Saturdays from now, teaching on how to overcome loneliness. This is a really important subject for modern people. There's so much loneliness, even in a big city — lots of people around, and people feel very lonely and isolated. It's so important to help people overcome this feeling of loneliness. And Kadam Holly is a wonderful teacher. If you haven't heard her teach before, she just has an incredible way about her, and so much experience both as a practitioner and teacher for many, many years — probably 30 years now as a practitioner, and another 25 as a teacher. So it's really an honor that she's coming here. I've claimed one of those front row seats, so don't you dare take my seat on that Saturday. I hope you can come and join in, even just to learn from a teaching skills point of view, to be inspired — how someone would approach and teach something like that, someone with so much skill and experience. It will be a lovely day. Okay, that's thing one — it's the 28th, two Saturdays from now.

Two, just a big thank you to everyone who helped make the empowerment happen in all the different ways that it did. There's probably maybe 25 people involved in some way — dealing with the copy, updating the website, sending out newsletters, putting out publicity, printing things, setting up the shrine, organizing the day, making the playlists, putting out the food, cleaning up, greeting people, registering people, and so on. There's so many people involved, and that's very inspiring. They feel like a network of kindness, and it creates a really positive energy. Everyone's involved in creating a beautiful event together as a community, as a sangha. I did talk to some people who are not from this center originally, and they were very inspired about being here. I think it was the people they met and the good hearts of everyone in our sangha that really touched them. So I think we can feel really delighted about that.

And then just a review of what we're doing. It was a while ago that we last had class — I think it was a snowy day. We were looking at working on our low-hanging delusion fruits. But that really meant trying to practice where we're at, and I even sent out on the WhatsApp a bunch of little tiny challenges. The idea was that they're actually simple, but sometimes we approach our practice in a very complicated and abstract way, and we're missing the point. What we really need to do is practice where we're at with our actual delusions, our actual problems, in our day-to-day life, and build some success there. So I'd love to hear any data — on that topic, or any of your own musings or anything you'd like to share or declare. I'd be happy to hear whatever, on topic or totally off topic. Dale and then Anne.

studentSharing.speaker: Dale
studentSharing.text:
So this is after your wonderful teachings yesterday on Heart Jewel. And I re-listened to the recording again this morning. And then I decided to go out for a walk, just a brief walk. And in my neighborhood — my God, there's so many people on the street, you could barely walk down the sidewalk on a weekend on the Upper West Side. And as I'm walking, I'm suddenly feeling, oh my goodness, all these people are suffering. All these people have problems. And it just — it wasn't from up in the head. It was from the heart. And I never felt that before in that way.

And so Je Tsongkhapa was walking with me. I mean, you talked about that in the teaching. I really felt like Je Tsongkhapa was taking a walk with me. And wouldn't it be wonderful if I would be able to help all these people? I mean, how many times have you said that? And it's like I heard it really in my heart for the first time. It was wonderful. I felt like I got a postcard from the Buddhas. So I took that in my heart and I still have that in my heart. Thank you.

studentSharing.speaker: Kadam Kyle
studentSharing.text: Thanks, Dale. That is delightful. You got some of Je Tsongkhapa's blessings, and then brought that into your day, and through remembering him at your heart in your day — going for a little walk with him — it gave you the blessing of a real great compassion, a powerful, beautiful great compassion. It's a rare mind, and it's a lovely, special mind to have. So what a nice blessing from the Wisdom Buddha, who is at one with Avalokiteshvara. Thank you so much. Anne, yes?

studentSharing.speaker: Anne
studentSharing.text:
I just wanted to shout out for the whole low-hanging fruit idea. After you set down that challenge, I wrote down every single little thing that disturbed my mind for about ten days. Then I fed it all into ChatGPT and said, what are the themes? And it came up with three. One I kind of knew — attachment to recognition and attention and wanting appreciation. One of them was just being disturbed by minor annoyances and inconveniences. And I'm like, all right, the wanting attention and recognition — that is not low-hanging fruit, that runs pretty deep. But these irritations seem like low-hanging fruit.

So I thought, what's my practice going to be? Something easy and quick. And I'm like, whenever I feel irritated — wonky mind, wonky world, right? What do you expect, Anne? What do you think your wonky mind is going to generate?

And what was interesting is, with this really simple practice every day, I kept noting down everything that disturbed me. I had many days in the last week where nothing disturbed me. I'm sure things did disturb me because I'm not an enlightened being, but nothing that was more than a little flicker, nothing that kind of reverberated through my day. And I was interested in how fast I was able to do that. To have a number of days within a two-week period where nothing bothered me, really, was very nice.

studentSharing.speaker: Kadam Kyle
studentSharing.text: Yeah, that's great. And could you say — just in a sentence — what was it that helped? Like, of all those little bits and pieces, what was it that really made the difference?

studentSharing.speaker: Anne
studentSharing.text: I guess it was a real determination and understanding there was nothing I could do. So why bother? Why even think about it? There's nothing I can do. This is how things are. And just really knowing that more and more deeply. Just don't fuss with it. Just move on. So my mind didn't get stuck on anything.

studentSharing.speaker: Kadam Kyle
studentSharing.text:
Yeah, it makes sense. It's the determination — that almost always is the principal subsequent factor in a Dharma practice actually really working for us. It's just a strong determination. Which is an incredibly unglamorous idea, but that's basically what it is. And my hunch is that the determination came from the clarity gained from really watching the mind and seeing the patterns. But I think you could have seen the pattern probably yourself, regardless, just from writing it down and catching all those thoughts.

A really powerful determination and a real clarity about what's going on in our mind — and then the flip side: not a powerful determination and a lack of clarity about what's really going on. I have a hunch that those two things are very closely related. More self-knowledge of understanding what's going on in our mind, more powerful determination. Thank you. Very nice. Others please. Adriana, yeah.

studentSharing.speaker: Adriana
studentSharing.text:
I think the teachings from the empowerment really complemented this assignment of the low-hanging fruit, because you encouraged us to have a plan. And my plan was to solve my inner problems rather than my outer problems. I came up with this phrase that's really helpful for me: this is my mind doing things to my mind. So good things, unpleasant things — everything is my mind doing things to my mind, not to Adriana, not to anyone else.

Every few days or once a week I'll call my mom, and it is the most unpleasant conversation — she really says horrible things about people, about the news, accusing me of all kinds of things. Usually I have to move the phone away from my ear, just like, it's going to be okay. But this very wonderful thing happened for the first time this past week where she said something, and I really experienced it as delightful. I felt so happy. And I was like, this is the only way to help my mom. My job is to just love my mom. Whatever is arising is happening from my mind.

It felt like a samsara glitch. But I really felt like, even in a bad habit with people — even a bad relationship for decades — if you really focus on applying Dharma, you can kind of blow it up and disappear it, even for a moment. So it really gives me faith that I can do that with everyone and everything.

studentSharing.speaker: Kadam Kyle
studentSharing.text: Thanks, Adriana. I love that you put the plan into action, working with inner problems, and then you had a specific strategy — just thinking, everything is the nature of my mind, coming from my mind — as a simple tool you can use over and over again. And you were able to apply it in real-life difficult situations, like chatting with mom. And then you got to see some movement there, which is exactly the idea. This is where our practice happens — with the people who are the main players in our life. That's where we want to apply our teachings. And as you said, it gives us a lot of faith. Thank you. Kristin, yes.

studentSharing.speaker: Kristin
studentSharing.text:
I just want to say thank you to everyone — it was a wonderful empowerment, really so special to be a part of it in all the ways. And I appreciated this task of focusing on a menial activity because I feel like I have so many things I have to do that I don't really want to do. Cleaning was a nice one I was working with. It's not perfect yet, but I definitely appreciated the assignment because it made it more relaxed and joyful, even if just a little.

But then interestingly, at the center — same task, right? But when we came to get ready for the empowerment, it really was that much more joyful. So it's really not the task at all, the activity. It really is your intention and what you're bringing to it.

And I'll say I was trying this again today, and my problem was this sort of time limitation and other pressures — I've got to do this, and also I have to have it finished by a certain time to get to the next thing. And cleaning often leads me to finding more things that are dirty. So if the time was endless, it wouldn't be so bad, but I need to get it done within this time. So I'm trying to instead focus on the wins — okay, it's better than it was. It's not perfect. It'll never be perfect, but it's better than it was. That's where I am.

studentSharing.speaker: Kadam Kyle
studentSharing.text:
Yeah, thank you very much. That's a really nice point, Kristin.

So we're talking about how one of these strategies is taking a menial task and trying to have a completely joyful mind in that task. Even though it's a simple idea, sometimes it can be very hard. And so you apply it to cleaning, and you notice a difference. It's not the cleaning itself — because cleaning at the Dharma Center with all these lovely people is a fun time, a big party. Cleaning at home, all the grimy stuff everywhere, not as fun.

And just noticing: it's not the cleaning itself. It's the mindset we bring to it. And also just the blessings of the center, for sure. But you did raise a really good point — we can investigate in these situations, what is the difference in the mindset? Part of the difference is a sense of time pressure. And then it's like: that's actually what's hard for me. It's not even cleaning. It's the time pressure. That's really interesting — that's not necessarily an easy thing to deal with, but it's clarifying what's really going on.

So the next practice would be: what would it be like to have a peaceful mind with a lot of time pressure in different parts of my life? What's it like to have a million things to do and no time to do them all, and have a peaceful mind? When we start practicing with seemingly menial tasks and trying to have a peaceful mind, we'll often notice a different layer of what's really going on. And that layer will be a really nice, right place for practice. And in the meantime, we can just rejoice that we're moving in the right direction. Yeah, so thanks so much, Kristin. Anyone else have anything they'd like to share or declare? Fran, yeah?

studentSharing.speaker: Fran
studentSharing.text:
I've been working on my perfectionism for a long time now and thought I was doing pretty well. I was making good progress and realizing that there's two kinds of perfectionists — the one that keeps going over and over until they get it right, or then there's me, that if I can't do it perfectly right away, I might as well not try. There have been circumstances in my life that have been forcing me to step up to the plate and do things out of my comfort zone. And my Heruka practice attacks my perfectionism in a couple of different ways, and it's been really great.

And then during the empowerment, there was something that I thought should have been my responsibility, but maybe I overlooked it. It turned out everything was fine, there were the right people in place. But during one of the meditations, I thought I had overlooked something, and it just destroyed me. I couldn't focus, and I tried to throw all my tools at it. And it just made me realize: I'm making progress, but I still have a long way to go. When the unexpected happens and I feel like it's my fault, I don't have the tools yet to really deal with it. I don't know how to find the middle way between being perfect and running away.

studentSharing.speaker: Kadam Kyle
studentSharing.text:
Yes, that's lovely, Fran. Thank you for sharing. It's not fun to face those minds and deal with them, but it's really lovely to see them. And it's kind of similar to the point in Kristin's data, and actually even Dale's data too — it's about getting that clarity about what's really going on.

For you, it's actually not just perfectionism — that's too vague a term. It's something about personal responsibility and letting people down. That's actually much more clear than perfectionism in general. And as we know our mind, we can start to zoom in more precisely. What exactly is going on here?

From one point of view, that can feel like we're going backwards, because it often really uproots us when we face one of those moments. But it's really not going backwards. We're moving forwards because we're seeing much more clearly and precisely what the challenge is in our mind.

I remember — we were at the Brazil temple setup, and I was using a good friend's car to transport food. It was this crazy Brazilian torrential rain, and I left the door open to grab the food and move it into the dining tent. There were like ten trays of food. And as I was doing that, he walked up to find his door open in his personal car, the water just pouring in. He was very, very upset. And later on, he noticed a scratch on it, which he assumed was my fault too — which it might have been, who knows.

And it was a great experience for me, because it was like, oh, I sort of thought I don't care that much what people think about me. But actually I really do, if it's someone who feels like a dear friend. He was just so mad, he wouldn't talk to me, wouldn't look at me, because he was dealing with other things and he was really upset. And the fact that I couldn't mediate the situation and solve it was really unpleasant. So it was helpful for me to clarify: the issue isn't exactly being liked or valued — it's more like not being able to solve a problem with a dear friend. Or not being valued by someone I really look up to. Anyway, just an example — these moments are clarifying, and they help us see what's really going on in our mind.

studentSharing.speaker: Ryan
studentSharing.text: So two weeks ago I almost had a beef with a friend when she announced there's not going to be a TTP two weeks ago.

studentSharing.speaker: Kadam Kyle
studentSharing.text: You have beef with me for that, yeah.

studentSharing.speaker: Ryan
studentSharing.text: And even though she's only the messenger, I had to give it up. So I almost had it with her — which is worth investigating, what exactly was my resentment. But I noticed that today I was thinking, you know what, I kind of got used to no TTP for two weeks. I wouldn't mind going home by 2 o'clock, just lying down, having a good book, a novel, and coffee, and just doing nothing. And that is worth investigating. I'm getting comfortable with my floor meditation, which is another thing to investigate.

studentSharing.speaker: Kadam Kyle
studentSharing.text:
Yeah, thanks Ryan. I think your point is that you're feeling more comfortable with your own kind of personal practice. And it's really nice — it's like I can become very reliant on the center, and it's nice to use the center and use it as a place of refuge. But it's also nice to reach a place where we can feel like the temple, the center, is in our heart. And it can go with us anywhere. The center is just an external manifestation of that. But ultimately, it's in our heart, and it can go with us everywhere we go.

And I think what you're also pointing out is about familiarity and habits. For me, I'm very reticent about ever canceling TTP, not because people don't need a break, but because it's just hard to build habits. It's hard. Once you have the habit going, it is infinitely easier to keep it going than to break it and then restart it. And it's just hard to restart a habit. Even over the summer, when we have little breaks, I notice it really affects people. Some people don't make it to the other side — the break happens, poof, and it's really moving to me to see that. That's the power of habits, the power of familiarity.

So when we do have these pauses, it's important in our own heart to think: this isn't actually a pause or a break from TTP. It's just a pause from being in the classroom, in the center. And I need to do something to create continuity in my own way — so we don't break that sense of movement and momentum. It might just be doing a little bit of practice at that same time, or a little bit of reading that day, or coming to the center in another fashion, or keeping up with a sangha friend, or talking about the text or doing a little studying. Whatever it is. These little habits really keep us afloat.

Fran's point about the Heruka practice — that's why that's a habit we really try to set as Kadampa Buddhists. Because it's something that is doable even when other things aren't. It's a habit, a win, that we can get even if nothing else is happening. And if we can keep that flowing, day after day, month after month, year after year, we're basically set. Everything else will come from that. We need some things that can be ingrained as positive, virtuous habits, even if the class isn't on. Okay, thanks so much. Let's get into the text.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, Precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace, You, who love all beings without exception, are the source of happiness and goodness. And you guide us to a liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded hands I turn to you, supreme unchanging friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you. May all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.

textStudy.speaker: Kadam Kyle
textStudy.text:
Okay, so we can take a look at the text. Page 55, in Benefits of Bodhichitta, starting at the paragraph, "At this point a doubt may arise."

At this point a doubt may arise. If, as stated, a Buddha has the ability to relieve all beings of their suffering, why have the countless Buddhas of the past not yet led everyone to enlightenment by now? The answer is as follows. Because Buddhas have overcome all obstructions and limitations, they possess all the wisdom, compassion and skillful means necessary for leading others to Buddhahood. However, if sentient beings from their own side do not exert the necessary effort — if they do not bother to follow the path shown to them by the Buddhas — they will remain stuck within samsara. As has often been said, a Buddha cannot remove another's suffering and delusions the way we can pluck a thorn from another's flesh. Without a cooperative effort, nothing can be achieved. Merely relying upon an enlightened being is not enough.

Okay, good to know. Maybe just to say one thing about this.

In Buddhist practice, we are always moving towards dependent relationship. Dependent relationship is the middle way. As we know, Je Tsongkhapa explained that dependent relationship is the best way to realize emptiness, understand emptiness. So dependent relationship is always cutting between extremes.

There are two extremes with respect to ourselves and Buddhas. Extreme one is thinking, Buddhas do it all, we do nothing, therefore I don't have to do anything — Buddhas are just going to do it. That's just a sort of passivity. Extreme two is thinking, I'm going to do everything. That's like a kind of solipsistic mindset — everything comes from my mind, me. That's just self-grasping ignorance masquerading as Buddhism. Some weird egotism, insane mindset.

So it's a cooperative relationship between us and the Buddhas, just as it's a cooperative relationship between us and everything. It's never all us. It's never all the Buddhas. There's always a dependent relationship, a connection. And that dependent relationship will always be a little bit invisible until we realize emptiness. But we want to keep moving towards that.

Practically, people in their own practice can be extreme in either of those ways. They can think, it's all me — and they can actually get disconnected from others, and the kindness of others, and the Buddhas. That's completely wrong. Even Buddhas rely on their spiritual guide. Look at Avalokiteshvara — he has Amitabha on his crown, and always shows the aspect of relying on a spiritual guide. It's a sense of dependent relationship.

And the other extreme is a kind of passivity — it's the Buddhas, they'll deal with it, they'll solve it. Or a far more diluted version is blaming other people: it's their fault, they've made all this mess for me.

So we're always going to lurch into different types of extremes until we realize emptiness perfectly. But until that day, it's just nice to be aware: where am I leaning? And how can I move a little bit more towards the middle way — definitely in our reliance on Buddhas?

For a lot of faiths, that answer is invisible. Many people conclude one or the other — either it's all you, no need for holy beings, just all you and your responsibility. Or all holy beings, all coming from some greater force — which is a very confusing place to be in, because it's hard to explain suffering when you conclude that. Anyway — Ben!

textStudy.speaker: Ben
textStudy.text: Just specifically, how does this apply to Phowa? How does it have an impact on the karma of someone who's not really aware what's happening?

textStudy.speaker: Kadam Kyle
textStudy.text:
Oh, yeah — you whack that beehive, Ben. Full rake. No, I'm just joking around. Yeah, these things are nice to ponder.

You can only understand Phowa through understanding the middle way. In Phowa practice, we're helping people go to the Pure Land. How can we help them go to the Pure Land if it's their karma whether they go or not? You can't change their karma. It's their karma. And Buddhas can't do it for them on their own. So these things can get a little confusing and awkward.

The more we think about emptiness, the more it will become clear. For example, there is no inherent other — that's one answer. So we do say generally speaking, their karma is their karma. But their karma is not inherently other. It's merely imputed karma. And there's no inherently existent owner of karma, because there's no inherently existent self. So the boundary lines between self and other aren't so rigid. If we look from the point of view of emptiness, those boundary lines dissolve very quickly. From the point of view of emptiness, that person is just merely imputed — so if we impute them as in the Pure Land, from that point of view, they're in the Pure Land. If we impute them as ordinary, they're ordinary. If we impute them as purified and in the Pure Land, they're purified and in the Pure Land. So that's definitely connected to the idea of the middle way.

From a more conventional point of view — just from the point of view of common appearance — it would be more like: they have a connection to the Buddhas, and we have a connection to the Buddhas that maybe is a bit stronger. And we're being a contributory factor, not a substantial cause, but a contributory cause, facilitating that connection. Similar to how, if someone we know is sick, they have the karma to meet a doctor — but maybe we're the person who drives them to that doctor. It's still their karma. We're just a contributory cause in facilitating that connection, not the principal cause, not the substantial cause. Those are three perspectives that are nice to ponder. Okay, one sentence, Fran.

textStudy.speaker: Fran
textStudy.text: Gen Kelsang Dekyong said that when we pray — and I view our prayers this way now — that we're creating the causes of what we're praying for. That prayer is a cause. So if we're praying for somebody to go to a Pure Land, we're creating the cause for them to go.

textStudy.speaker: Kadam Kyle
textStudy.text:
Yeah, yeah, thank you. So a few ideas for you, Ben. Thank you.

Okay, very good. So then Shantideva continues by advising us how to behave towards a Bodhisattva. He quotes Buddha Shakyamuni as having said that one moment of anger directed towards a Bodhisattva — this peerless benefactor of all sentient beings — contaminates the mind with an enormous non-virtuous residue. As a result, we'll abide in an intensely suffering realm of the hell beings for as many aeons as there were moments of anger.

So we should just all quit now, because we've all done that. Right, should we just quit? Abandon our practice? It's too late — we've already created this cause, so it's all over for us. We should just get discouraged and quit.

So I'm making this point because we have to be so clear about how we use the Dharma. The Dharma is designed to help us overcome our delusions. So whenever we read a sentence, we need to ask: how am I going to use this to overcome my delusions, to make my delusions less? We want to use that as a filter always. All Dharma is designed to do that. We never, ever want to use Dharma to increase our delusions. You can use any line to increase your delusions — you can use something like this to make yourself very discouraged. Oh my gosh, I have all this karma to go to hell because I've been so angry at Bodhisattvas — I should just give up. Why would you think that? That's just increasing delusion.

So this is an important filter to always have — like a lens, a magnifying glass, a prism — to look through any Dharma teaching: how can I use this to decrease my delusions? So for example with this teaching, I'm going to decrease my lack of regret for my negative actions, and I'm going to wish to purify some more — which is a very virtuous mind. Or I'm going to use this to make sure I'm very mindful of how I think about a Bodhisattva, or anyone, because anyone can be a Bodhisattva.

When we're teaching Dharma, we have to be careful about this too. I don't look at things like this in a way that makes me discouraged — it's not how I've ever looked at Dharma. So I like thinking about hell, and all the suffering in hell that I might get into if I keep up my non-virtue. But I have to be very careful, because some people find that very discouraging. So even though it's very comfortable and inspiring for me to think about that infinite non-virtue in my mind that I need to purify, when I'm teaching a class I have to be thinking: are these people going to hear this in a way that helps them reduce their delusions, or will it increase them?

But since we're all in the TTP, we should be trying to do this ourselves — not making sure someone else does this for us. We need to take a bit of responsibility: never ever use a class, a teaching, whatever, to increase our delusions. And sometimes we have to be very mindful. What's going on in my mind? How am I seeing this teaching? How can I make sure I use this for what I need today?

Yeah, okay. However, if we generate a virtuous mind — such as faith towards a Bodhisattva — the fruits of this action will multiply even more abundantly than the results of an angry mind. While anger towards a Bodhisattva is thousands of times more non-virtuous than anger towards an ordinary being, faith in a Bodhisattva is far more meritorious than faith in an ordinary object. Phew! Now we're all good.

Bodhichitta has so many good qualities and leads to so many beneficial results that the body of one who has developed this supremely precious mind is worthy to be an object of our prostrations. In one of his previous lifetimes as a Bodhisattva, Buddha Shakyamuni appeared as King Maitribala. Yeah, this is a great story.

He was wise, charitable, and well-loved by his subjects, and soon his fame spread far and wide. Eventually news of this king reached the abode of five cannibalistic demons. Boo! They became very jealous of his good qualities and as a result plotted to murder him — as five cannibalistic demons would do. It's like one of their main activities, plotting to murder people. A little coven of demons.

Knowing his reputation for generosity, they appeared before him and begged for charity. The king immediately gave them much gold and silver, but instead of accepting this, they replied, this is an inappropriate offering — we are cannibals, so please give us your flesh and blood. The king assented to this gruesome request, and as he gave them some of his blood, he prayed: as I am now satisfying them with my blood, may I one day satisfy them with pure Dharma and thereby be of true benefit to them.

When this king was later reborn as Buddha Shakyamuni, these five demons were reborn as his first disciples. After listening to Buddha's first discourse delivered in Sarnath — initiating the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma — these five became Arhats, attaining complete personal liberation from all suffering. Thus, even to those who do them harm, Bodhisattvas return temporary and ultimate joy and benefit. Since these Bodhisattvas are the foundation for all sentient beings' happiness, it is appropriate that we take continuous refuge in them.

So we can ask ourselves: who are my cannibalistic demons of my life? Hopefully just five, but you might have ten or a hundred. It's nice to label them that. Greetings, cannibalistic demon! It's very fun to ponder our little cannibalistic demons of our life. They're just appearances to our mind, and one day they're going to be our main disciples — when we appear as a Buddha. They're our cannibalistic demons. They're not someone else's. They're our little personal demons. We snuggle them in. They live in our pocket. Five little demons that we bring around with us. And they're going to be our disciples one day.

So it's good to work on it now. I'm sure we were all cannibalistic demons for some Buddha at some point, all working together to try to murder them. I don't know who was the ringleader, but one of us was. And now we're here together, studying and meditating together. We came a long way from demonhood.

So this is a very important practical teaching — with respect to this prayer. And it's related to what Fran said, that prayer is a cause, that it's actively helping people. And it's a little bit related to Sumit's point earlier, about how can we feel we're making a difference when it just seems like a karmic difference. Can we really feel that the karmic differences we're making are a real difference? Somewhat yes, and somewhat no, and we can all grow this a little bit. But practicing this thought is a great way to start to deepen this — really having this long game, and thinking about people's future lives.

So we're not necessarily making this exact prayer — as I am now satisfying them with my blood, may I one day satisfy them with pure Dharma. But you just plug in the thing that you're not exactly delighted about doing with them as the first part, and finish up the second part. As I am now listening to them tell this story for the tenth time in a row — like as our aging parents age, and we've all been there. Maybe it's our spouse, maybe it's a friend who just keeps going on about their highlights from their youth, and we've heard it a million times. As I am listening to this story for the hundredth time, may I one day satisfy this person with pure Dharma, and thereby be of true benefit to them.

And it's a mindfulness practice. What we're trying to get to is a feeling of delight in that conversation. Or there's some bureaucratic nightmare — you're on hold, or getting yelled at by someone behind a counter, whatever. As I now am in this situation, may I one day give them pure Dharma and really be of benefit to them.

It's important too as Dharma teachers — when we come to the Dharma Center, we'll meet students who come, and maybe we'd love to talk about Dharma, and maybe our class is really inspiring, and then they just want to talk about ordinary things. And it's tempting to try to redirect the conversation — which sometimes works. But sometimes what we need to do is just make this prayer. As we now talk about whatever, may one day we talk about pure Dharma together, and discuss the union of the two truths together, and discuss how to develop great bliss and emptiness together.

So this is a bit about demons — our personal cannibalistic demons. Earlier we had a teaching skills class — which everyone in TTP is invited to — and we were talking about how do you lead people to have faith in the Three Jewels. And one thing to remember is this word Dharma. It means to hold back. Protection is one translation, but to hold back is actually the most precise translation of Dharma — to hold back from the suffering of the lower realms especially, but also of samsaric suffering, and eventually of having self-cherishing. These are the three scopes of the Lamrim.

So it's interesting to think: when we think about Dharma, does it have this implicit meaning of at least being about holding back suffering in the lower realms? Because if it's about just this life, Dharma is not designed to do that. It's not about happiness in this life — that's a side effect that's really nice, but it really is not about that at all. It's about, at the very least, the bare minimum aim: to help ourselves or others be free of suffering in future lives.

I find this very helpful to think about, because the Dharma can help us in the here and now, and it's so easy for us to think about it in that context — essentially as a psychological salve for the pains of modern life, like it just softens the blow of living a modern, miserable life. And it can help with that, definitely. But that's not the intention at all. The intention is, at least, to help people become free of the suffering of future lives, and hopefully to become free of samsaric suffering, and at most to become a Buddha.

So when we think about this word Dharma, and having faith in Dharma, we want to remember: that's the bare minimum aim we're going for in our Dharma practice — freedom from suffering in future lives. Attaining happiness in this life isn't even at the bare minimum. It is below the bare minimum. It is underneath the least aim.

So when we're making a prayer like this — as we do this, may one day I give you Dharma — we're having a very long-term view, and we're trying to feed this long-term mindset. A many-lives mindset, which is hard to inhabit in these days. It's not emulated by a lot of people we know. It's not in the movies we see. People aren't talking about future lives a lot. And so we want to just make sure we keep feeding this understanding in ourselves. And making a prayer like this is actually helping a lot — just like Buddha helped his cannibalistic demons so that one day they could be his disciples in future lives, may I help these people in the future. And we're even feeling like that's enough. That's a good enough wish.

I just wanted to share that a little bit because of our teaching skills class, and thinking about this word Dharma — making sure we're attuned to that. We know the Lamrim. The initial scope is designed to help us attain freedom from suffering in future lives — to hold us back from lower rebirth. That's what it's designed to do. That's the bare minimum.

Although there are numerous Mahayana practices of both Sutra and Tantra, there is no practice more important than Bodhichitta. By following the path of Tantra it is possible to attain enlightenment in one short lifetime. However, if we have not developed Bodhichitta, it does not matter how much or for how long we practise — it will be utterly impossible to attain enlightenment. Thus it is a great mistake to think that since Tantra is the quick path to enlightenment, we should enter into it immediately and completely forget about developing Bodhichitta. Such a misguided way of practising Dharma will be completely empty of results.

It is extremely important to follow the spiritual path correctly and gradually, without omitting any of its stages. To train our mind in this way is to emulate the examples of such great practitioners as Milarepa, who attained enlightenment in one lifetime. Milarepa once said: First I feared the eight states of bondage. I meditated on impermanence, death, and the shortcomings of samsara. I observed very carefully the law of actions and their effects, and relied solely upon the Three precious and sublime Jewels of refuge. For a long time I trained in the two methods for developing Bodhichitta. Later I came to see that whatever appeared to my mind lacked true existence and was like an illusion. Now I have no fear of rebirth in the lower realms. Such a well-ordered method of practice should be our guide as we follow the Bodhisattva path.

This concludes the Benefits of Bodhichitta — the first chapter of Meaningful to Behold, the commentary to Shantideva's Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life.

This is just encouragement to practice the Lamrim. Which we can all ask — how is our Lamrim practice going? Do we love it? Do we love each of the 21 meditations? In the depths of our heart, we're just excited. Does the hair stand up on the back of our neck when we think about each of the 21 meditations, because it's so thrilling? So we can ask ourselves that a little bit.

There is no path to enlightenment that we can follow without us at some point realizing the Lamrim is so important. We don't have to understand that today, but what we need to understand is that there will be a day where we conclude that. And until that day comes, our path is a little bit closed up. Which is okay, but it's a bit of a bummer. And we should get moving on it to see the value of the Lamrim. There are blockages that are impossible to penetrate in our mind without penetrating the meditations of the Lamrim.

textStudy.speaker: Kadam Kyle
textStudy.text:
And so the best day to love the Lamrim is like yesterday, or a while ago. But the second best day is basically today. And after that, tomorrow.

So I'm just encouraging us a little bit to think about it. From one point of view, in our practice we use our wisdom and we talk with our spiritual guide, and we figure out — okay, this is what I need, this is what I want to practice. And that's very nice, to have a little bit of a personalized touch. But if that doesn't somehow deeply include the Lamrim, we didn't listen to our spiritual guide. Because they would never ever say, don't do the Lamrim. They would never say that — because that's the entire spiritual path.

Sometimes I'll meet people and they'll say, I don't know what practice to do. I don't know what to emphasize. Ah, there's so many practices. And it's very interesting, because actually there's always been an answer: you should do the Lamrim. If you don't think you should do it, I hope you have a special dispensation of some sort that you've come up with through conversing with your spiritual guide. Lamrim means the stages of the path to enlightenment. What kind of spiritual path involves not meditating on the stages of the path to enlightenment?

For me, I was taught from day one when I first started practicing: you do your Heruka practice, and you do your Lamrim meditation, every day, until you die. And I've never regretted that. I've never heard better advice. Basically, everyone I know who's had a very long, flourishing practice — if I ask them, what do you exactly do? You know what they say? I do a Heruka practice, or Hundreds of Deities of the Joyful Land according to Highest Yoga Tantra, or some derivation of that, and Lamrim meditation. Everyone that has actually done something inspiring. When I meet people who are very conflicted and struggling in their practice, I've never asked them what they're doing and had them say, Heruka and Lamrim — every day. There's never an overlap there. So it's very interesting.

Anyway, I'm just raving about this — my own little bone to pick. But that's what I've seen personally. And of course, maybe we have some special reason to do something else, and we can chat with our spiritual guide, and if there's a reason, great. We have freedom. We can do whatever we'd like. But it's a good question — why is that better than doing Heruka and Lamrim meditation?

So please don't use that to discourage yourself. Don't develop delusions when you think about Dharma — we already talked about that. Instead, maybe we can develop some admiring faith in the Lamrim and think, why is that core to our practice? Okay, very good.

Let's have a little time for discussion now. I'll choose the groups today. Let's have Mimi and Mary Ann. And Ryan and Anne. And Fran, Sumit, and Anne P. Thank you.

postDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postDiscussion.text: All right, welcome back, y'all. Anyone have anything they'd like to share or declare about the discussion? Any musings or poetic ramblings or whatever else you got?

postDiscussion.speaker: Anne
postDiscussion.text: I have not been studying the Lamrim.

postDiscussion.speaker: Anne
postDiscussion.text: I'm going to. I have a plan. I have a commitment.

postDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postDiscussion.text:
I love it. You can be one of the people who carves on a tree in Brooklyn — you know, A plus L, Anne plus Lamrim, with a little heart around it. So that's also part of your plan, hopefully.

We do want to get to that place where we're just like, Lamrim — oh yeah, salivating, thinking about how thrilling it is. That's kind of where we'd like to get to. It'd be very nice. Adriana, yeah.

postDiscussion.speaker: Adriana
postDiscussion.text: For a meditation break practice — I remember one time after leaving a retreat, Gen Samten said that when we go home and brush our teeth, we could just think, I'm brushing my teeth for the benefit of all. Like putting my shoes on for the benefit of all. And Neil mentioned taking out the garbage and thinking you're purifying all impure environments. So we got inspired by Buddha Shakyamuni as the king making that intention. Practicing — in a light and fun way — transforming ordinary activities into really meaningful causes.

postDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postDiscussion.text: Yeah, that sounds good. Bringing that prayer that he had towards the cannibals, but into every activity. It's a great mindfulness practice. Very nice. Do all yogas by one — I think that's what Geshe-la says. Anything else? Fran, yes.

postDiscussion.speaker: Fran
postDiscussion.text: I like the idea of remembering that Dharma isn't for this life — that it's for future lives, for myself and for everybody else. And to, you know, may someday we study Dharma together, but nothing about now.

postDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postDiscussion.text: Yeah. Thank you. It's an important step. And that's actually one of the functions of Lamrim — to move us into being a special small scope being who thinks, may my practice go towards my future lives. And it doesn't even matter if it happens in this life. May it just go towards my happiness of future lives. And the more we inhabit that mindset, basically the more we relax deeply, and then our practice will really take off.

postDiscussion.speaker: Fran
postDiscussion.text: It made me think about the Tara Mantra, because I say mantras for people suffering in this life, but the real meaning of it is — please protect me from lower rebirth, please protect me from samsaric rebirth, please help me become enlightened.

postDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postDiscussion.text:
Yeah, exactly. The three parts of the Tara Mantra are reflected in the three scopes of Lamrim, because Tara was Atisha's guide and helped him discover and teach the Lamrim. So her mantra is imbued with those three scopes, as you said.

It's interesting — when we wish people just happiness in this life, it's like thinking about someone with cancer who's suffering profoundly and just thinking, I want you to have happiness tomorrow. Well, what about the day after that? It just doesn't even make that much sense. No — I want you to have happiness, I want you to be totally free of this suffering, this pain. So when we wish for happiness in this life, for ourselves, for others, it's basically like that same idea. Actually it's even less than that — it's more like, I wish you happiness for one second, because the ratio of seconds in this life to the rest of countless future lives is staggering. Yeah. Dale, yes.

postDiscussion.speaker: Dale
postDiscussion.text: This really comes out of your teaching, but I love the idea of doing everything with Je Tsongkhapa at your heart, steering you, guiding you. I think it helps dispel loneliness and feeling like — well, what am I doing? It's beautiful.

postDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postDiscussion.text: Yeah. Can't go wrong with that, Dale. And honestly, if we keep Je Tsongkhapa at our heart, we'll naturally move towards the Lamrim, we'll naturally destroy all the delusions, we'll naturally develop Bodhichitta, and so on. So it's a wonderful practice to get into. Okay. Mary Ann, last one, yeah, and then we'll wrap it up.

postDiscussion.speaker: Mary Ann
postDiscussion.text: It also came out of the workshop yesterday — combining play with your practice. So I thought I would just make a drawing of the Lamrim meditations, because I've never done them in order — true confession. And just sit there with that thing on my lap and look at it. Like, there it is. That's impermanence and death as an image.

postDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postDiscussion.text:
That's fantastic, Mary Ann. Instead of thinking of it as, I'm going to meditate on each topic each day, just think, I'm going to draw the Lamrim meditation for the day. So you do precious human life, you just make a little drawing of it. And the next day, death, make a little drawing of it. And the next day, the dangers of rebirth, make a little drawing of it. And if you just keep it there, it'd be very playful and fun, and it's in line with what you love to do. But you'll definitely be thinking about the meditation by putting it into an image — it'll just be speaking to you in that way, because that's how your mind works. So it's nice to bring in some play, as you mentioned.

Okay, very good. So we can just finish with a dedication now. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing — may all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications. Okay, thank you. Thanks, everyone.
